title: Redwood Private VPC Security Architecture deep dive with Harbor Bank
next_steps: Redwood: share SOC 2 Type II and ISO27001 summaries + Private deployment runbook (link)
Harbor: export current VPC/net ACLs and CIDRs and share with Redwood
Schedule in-lab benchmarking for egress/ingress throughput on private cluster (week of 2026-12-20)
Set up follow-up deep dive on KMS integration with Harbor KMS (14 days)
Agree on pilot timeline and send draft MSA / security addendum
action_items: Liam Chen: Send SOC2 summary, ISO artifacts, and private-vpc runbook link - due 2026-12-15
Priya Kapoor: Prepare recommended network diagram and example firewall rules for Harbor's CIDR - due 2026-12-14
Daniel Wu: Share current VPC CIDRs, existing peering, and NAT/gateway config - due 2026-12-13
Samantha Lee: Provide list of logging/SIEM endpoints (Splunk ids) and retention requirements - due 2026-12-13
Noah Patel: Confirm whether Harbor requires air-gapped option or can accept VPC with restricted egress - due 2026-12-17
transcript: 00:00:02 Liam Chen: All right folks, thanks for joining. Quick roll call; we'll do a security and network deep dive on the Redwood Private VPC offering, focusing on network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, KMS and audit logs. I'm Liam, AE. Priya is our security SE, Ethan is on solutions and Zoe is CSM. 00:00:22 Maria Torres: Hi all, Maria here, CISO at Harbor Bank. We have Daniel, Sam, Noah on the call. We're mainly evaluating Private / VPC deployment, SOC2/ISO posture and how Redwood will integrate with our KMS and SIEM. 00:00:35 Priya Kapoor: Thanks Maria. Quick agenda: 1) high-level architecture; 2) network isolation and ingress/egress controls; 3) identity and access (SSO, RBAC); 4) encryption, KMS; 5) logging/audit and compliance artifacts. We'll leave time at the end for Q&A. 00:00:50 Daniel Wu: Sounds good. We're particularly concerned about egress - we have strict data exfiltration rules and need to ensure minimal outbound connectivity. 00:01:05 Priya Kapoor: Totally get that. At a high level our Private deployment can be in your VPC (VPC-hosted mode) or as an on-prem package. For Harbor you've indicated wanting a customer VPC with dedicated subnets for Redwood compute and control plane. That means all compute nodes are inside your subnets and network policies are enforced by your firewalls. 00:01:30 Samantha Lee: Quick clarification: control plane - is that in Redwood's account or in our account? 00:01:36 Liam Chen: Good question. We offer two models: 1) shared control plane (hosted control plane) with private endpoints into your VPC, or 2) fully private control plane deployed in your account - that latter is the Private/air-gapped/on-prem option. For Harbor, given compliance, we're recommending the control plane be customer-managed in your account. 00:01:58 Maria Torres: We prefer customer-managed control plane. We need full auditability and don't want management plane telemetry leaving our tenancy unless it's encrypted and logged. 00:02:12 Priya Kapoor: Understood. In customer-managed control plane mode we deploy our control components into your management subnets; we provide Terraform modules and runbooks. All management traffic stays in your VPC, and we support VPC endpoints so there's no public internet egress for control traffic. 00:02:30 Noah Patel: When you say VPC endpoints, do you mean AWS PrivateLink or Interface endpoints? 00:02:36 Priya Kapoor: Yes, for AWS we typically recommend Interface VPC Endpoints (PrivateLink) for service connections like S3, Secrets Manager, KMS if accessible via VPC endpoints; we can also use Gateway endpoints for S3. For on-prem we rely on direct connect / private peering. 00:02:55 Daniel Wu: What about NAT - do your compute nodes require outbound internet via NAT for model downloads or telemetry? 00:03:03 Ethan Ramos: Great question. We try to avoid outbound model pulls at runtime. For Private, you either pre-stage model artifacts into your S3 or your internal artifact store. That eliminates runtime egress for model downloads. Telemetry and metrics are configurable - you can route them to your own metrics/monitoring endpoints via VPC endpoints; we can also disable telemetry to Redwood's hosted endpoints if needed. 00:03:25 Samantha Lee: And if we need to lock egress completely, is there an air-gapped option? 00:03:30 Priya Kapoor: Yes. We have an air-gapped on-prem deployment where all artifacts are preloaded and there's zero outbound. That requires more support during onboarding and patching, but it's an option for high-regulated environments. 00:03:43 Maria Torres: Okay. Let's dig into firewalling: how are the security groups and NACLs expected to be configured? Do you provide sample rules? 00:03:50 Priya Kapoor: We provide a recommended baseline: separate subnets for control plane, compute, and training/ML storage. Security groups are least-privilege: control plane SG only allows inbound from admin IP ranges and from compute SG on specific ports (gRPC, 443, 8443). Compute SG allows inbound from internal load balancers and control plane, outbound blocked by default except to internal artifact stores or to specific VPC endpoints. We will share an example ruleset in the runbook. 00:04:17 Daniel Wu: Can you put a WAF in front of the public endpoints? We have requirements to inspect incoming traffic and block certain patterns. 00:04:23 Priya Kapoor: Absolutely. You can front the endpoints with your WAF (AWS WAF / Cloudflare) and only allow traffic from vetted ALBs. For private deployments there usually aren't public endpoints - though the admin console can be exposed via CIDR-restricted ALB with WAF. 00:04:38 Samantha Lee: For ingress, we want only specific partner IPs allowed for tracing/backups. Is that feasible? 00:04:44 Ethan Ramos: Yes - we support allowlists on the ALB and security group level. We also support TLS client certs and mTLS between services if you want extra assurance. 00:04:55 Maria Torres: Let's talk identity - SSO and RBAC. We use Okta with SCIM for user provisioning. 00:05:02 Priya Kapoor: Okta is standard. We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM for provisioning. Roles are mapped from your IdP groups to Redwood roles, and we support fine-grained RBAC for project-level access. For audit and privileged actions we can show you the full event stream. 00:05:20 Daniel Wu: Are there built-in privileged account protections - like session recording, just-in-time admin? 00:05:26 Zoe Martin: We support integration with SSO for MFA enforcement; we also support ephemeral admin tokens and can integrate with your PAM for elevated operations. Session recording is available in the admin console audit logs - we log admin API calls and console UI changes with user context. 00:05:44 Samantha Lee: Good. On encryption: we use our own KMS - Harbor KMS with key policies controlled by our security team. Can Redwood integrate with a customer KMS? 00:05:54 Priya Kapoor: Yes. For AWS we integrate with customer-managed CMKs in your account. We support encrypting volumes and S3 with CMKs. For other providers we support KMIP/HSM integrations and can also support Azure Key Vault or GCP KMS depending on deployment. We also support envelope encryption where Redwood handles the data key but the master key is in your KMS. 00:06:17 Daniel Wu: How do you handle secrets for model weights and API keys inside the cluster? 00:06:22 Ethan Ramos: Secrets should live in your secret manager (Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault). Our runtime pulls ephemeral secrets via private endpoints and caches them in memory with limited lifetime; we do not persist plaintext secrets to disk. We also support sealed-secrets workflows for on-prem. 00:06:40 Maria Torres: On audit logs: we need immutable logs forwarded to our Splunk instance - retention 7 years for certain event classes. 00:06:48 Priya Kapoor: We can forward logs via VPC endpoints to your logging collector. For Splunk we typically send over HTTP Event Collector (HEC) on a private network path or through a syslog forwarder in your VPC. Logs include API calls, admin actions, model invocation traces (token-level tracing is optional and can be redacted). We sign and timestamp logs; for immutability you can route them to an S3 bucket with object lock enabled. 00:07:15 Samantha Lee: Token-level traces - we can't have raw PII/token content going to any third party. How do you redact? 00:07:21 Priya Kapoor: By default we do not send user input payloads to Redwood-hosted telemetry. For audit we can emit high-level invocation metadata (request id, model id, latencies) but you can opt-in to more detailed traces and we provide redaction hooks so PII patterns are scrubbed before logs leave the cluster. 00:07:40 Daniel Wu: Any support for SIEM correlation - for example including request ids that map to our transaction ids? 00:07:46 Ethan Ramos: Yes - you can pass correlation ids in headers and our logs will include them. That helps with end-to-end tracing in your SIEM. 00:07:55 Maria Torres: About network egress: we need to make sure there's no unnoticed DNS exfil. Does Redwood support restricting DNS resolution or private DNS? 00:08:04 Priya Kapoor: We recommend using your VPC resolver (Route 53 Resolver) and restrict outbound DNS to your resolvers only. We also support DNS resolvers in our on-prem package. Additionally, egress is handled by NACLs/Security Groups and we suggest black-holing unknown destinations at the NAT/Firewall layer. 00:08:22 Daniel Wu: What about kernel-level telemetry or side-channels - anything we should be aware of? 00:08:28 Priya Kapoor: Our runtime is user-space and we avoid requiring host-level kernel modules. For on-prem you will control the host; we provide a checklist for hardening (disable unused services, kernel patching cadence, host IDS). 00:08:40 Samantha Lee: Patch cadence - how often are runtime and model updates applied? 00:08:45 Zoe Martin: For private customer-managed we recommend monthly security patches; critical CVEs are patched out-of-band. For air-gapped customers we coordinate patch windows. We document CVEs and provide patch manifests. 00:08:59 Maria Torres: Can we do an attestation or a baseline security scan prior to production go-live? 00:09:05 Priya Kapoor: Yes. We do third-party pentests and we can share a redacted report. We also support you running an internal pentest; we provide a test plan and allowed IP ranges. 00:09:16 Daniel Wu: On the network side, can you support Transit Gateway peering? We have multiple accounts across OU and want centralized connectivity. 00:09:23 Ethan Ramos: We integrate with Transit Gateway and account peering. Our Terraform modules include TGW attachments and route table examples. We also support hub-and-spoke designs. 00:09:34 Samantha Lee: For monitoring we use Datadog. Can Redwood emit metrics there? 00:09:38 Priya Kapoor: Yes - we can push metrics via private endpoints to Datadog, or you can run an agent in your VPC that scrapes the endpoints. We support tagging for observability. 00:09:50 Maria Torres: About compliance artifacts - can you provide SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 certificates and a penetration test summary? 00:09:58 Liam Chen: Yes, we'll share a SOC2 Type II summary and an ISO27001 certificate; we often provide a redacted penetration test report under NDA. We'll attach those to the runbook link. 00:10:10 Daniel Wu: One place we often get stuck: when Redwood components need IAM roles in our account - principle of least privilege. Do you provide role templates? 00:10:18 Priya Kapoor: We provide IAM role templates and least-privilege policies. For example, a role for S3 read to specific buckets, KMS decrypt on specific CMKs, and no broad *:*. We also provide a readme for permission boundaries. 00:10:30 Samantha Lee: For KMS key policies, do we need to add Redwood principals to the CMK? 00:10:35 Priya Kapoor: If you want Redwood-managed services to call the KMS on your behalf, then yes you'd add a service principal or role ARN to the key policy. Alternatively, you can use envelope encryption where Redwood never has direct KMS decrypt permissions - we handle data keys encrypted by your master key and we only operate on ciphertext. We can walk through tradeoffs. 00:10:55 Daniel Wu: Can you show an example in the runbook? 00:10:57 Priya Kapoor: Absolutely - we'll include example key policies for both patterns. 00:11:05 Maria Torres: For legal/procurement we will need a security addendum in the MSA that includes breach notification windows. What are Redwood's SLAs? 00:11:13 Liam Chen: For Dedicated and Private we have enterprise SLAs we can tailor; breach notification windows are standard 72 hours for confirmed incidents and we can contract stricter timelines in the addendum. 00:11:24 Samantha Lee: Can we get a copy of the standard addendum to review? 00:11:27 Zoe Martin: Yes, we'll share the standard security addendum with the next steps. 00:11:33 Daniel Wu: Network segmentation: do you recommend host-level microsegmentation as well or is SG/NACL enough? 00:11:40 Priya Kapoor: Security groups and NACLs are the baseline. If you need defense-in-depth we recommend host-level microsegmentation (e.g., using a service mesh or host firewall) especially for east-west traffic between multi-tenant workloads. For Redwood workloads running in dedicated subnets it's usually sufficient, but we support adding a service mesh for zero-trust. 00:11:58 Maria Torres: What about data residency - our customers in EMEA require data to remain in EU regions. Can you pin region? 00:12:05 Liam Chen: Yes, you can pin model serving to specific regions and we support region-restricted storage. For Private deployments in your account you control the region. For hosted offerings we offer EU-only regions. 00:12:17 Daniel Wu: About backward compatibility - if we rotate KMS keys, how do you handle existing artifacts? 00:12:22 Priya Kapoor: We support key rotation with envelope encryption; when you rotate the CMK the data keys are re-wrapped, and we provide tooling to re-encrypt artifacts in your object stores. We'll include the rotation playbook. 00:12:36 Samantha Lee: Regarding egress monitoring, can Redwood emit egress flow logs? 00:12:41 Ethan Ramos: We can emit VPC Flow Logs and application-level egress logs. Flow logs can be pushed to your chosen logs pipeline and we can alert on anomalous destinations. 00:12:52 Maria Torres: For defense-in-depth, do you recommend IDS/IPS? 00:12:55 Priya Kapoor: Yes. We recommend host IDS and network IDS (Suricata, GuardDuty). For on-prem you can run Zeek or Suricata and feed into Splunk. We provide recommended detection rules. 00:13:10 Daniel Wu: Any guidance on secrets rotation for model credentials? 00:13:15 Priya Kapoor: Rotate secrets frequently; we recommend short TTLs and avoid long-lived keys. Use automated rotation in Secrets Manager or Vault with leases. 00:13:25 Maria Torres: Ok, we want to run a benchmark that simulates our production traffic with out-of-hours windows. How do we safely run load tests without sending PII? 00:13:32 Ethan Ramos: We can run synthetic datasets, or run an anonymization step before sending. We also support in-cluster transforms that sanitize data prior to telemetry emission. We'll coordinate the load window and test plan. 00:13:44 Daniel Wu: A couple of specific questions from our architects: 1) will the runtime open ephemeral outbound connections to model repos or container registries? 2) how are kernel upgrades handled if you're running our hosts? 00:13:54 Priya Kapoor: 1) Not at runtime if you pre-stage artifacts. 2) Host kernel upgrades are controlled by you; we recommend a maintenance window and we provide guidance on safe drain/evacuation of workloads. 00:14:06 Maria Torres: We have a question about multi-tenancy - can we run multiple Harbor teams with strict project boundaries? 00:14:12 Priya Kapoor: Yes - RBAC and network isolation per project. Each project can have dedicated subnets and IAM roles for least privilege. 00:14:22 Samantha Lee: Let's talk timeline: if we sign next week how long to pilot? 00:14:27 Liam Chen: Typical pilot (private-VPC) is 4-6 weeks: provisioning, artifacts staging, smoke tests, and one week of production-like validation. Air-gapped may add 2-3 weeks. 00:14:36 Daniel Wu: Can we run a joint tabletop exercise for incident response? 00:14:40 Zoe Martin: Yes, we do run tabletop IR sessions with customers. We'll propose an agenda. 00:14:48 Maria Torres: Anything else about regulatory? We need audit trails for trader communications - anything special? 00:14:54 Priya Kapoor: For regulated data classes we recommend stricter logging retention, object lock for S3 audit buckets, and restricted access to model invocation traces. We can tag requests with business context for audit and retention policies. 00:15:10 Daniel Wu: A couple more nitty-gritty items: can you support mutual TLS for internal service-to-service calls? 00:15:16 Priya Kapoor: Yes, mTLS is supported for internal traffic and for inbound admin APIs. We support cert rotation using your PKI. 00:15:24 Samantha Lee: For backups of model state and KV caches, where do those live and how are those encrypted? 00:15:29 Ethan Ramos: Backups are stored in your object store and encrypted with your CMKs. Backup lifecycle and retention are configurable. For KV caches we support snapshotting to S3 and those snapshots are encrypted at rest. 00:15:40 Maria Torres: Ok, can you list the major artifacts we'll get in the runbook? 00:15:44 Priya Kapoor: Runbook will include: architecture diagram, Terraform modules, IAM policies, security group/NACL examples, KMS key policy examples, logging pipeline configs for Splunk/Datadog, patch/upgrade playbook, and on-prem install checklist. We'll share a link post-call. 00:16:00 Daniel Wu: Please include a sample ALB rule set and WAF rules. 00:16:04 Priya Kapoor: Will do. 00:16:08 Samantha Lee: On the sandbox: can we get read-only access first for the compliance team? 00:16:12 Liam Chen: Yes - we can provision a read-only tenant scoped to compliance reviewers. 00:16:17 Maria Torres: Great. For change control, how do we track config drift? 00:16:21 Priya Kapoor: We recommend running the Terraform modules in an org-wide pipeline and using drift detection; we support configuration as code and we provide recommended IaC patterns. 00:16:33 Daniel Wu: Okay that covers most of it. Any outstanding security concerns from Redwood side? 00:16:38 Priya Kapoor: Just the typical - ensure your NAT/firewall posture blocks unknown egress, KMS policies are tightened, and logging retention meets your compliance. We'll give specifics in the runbook. 00:16:48 Maria Torres: Let's recap next steps. 00:16:51 Liam Chen: Recap: Redwood will send SOC2/ISO artifacts, runbook link, example network diagrams and IAM templates; schedule benchmarking week of 12/20; we will share security addendum and pilot timeline. Harbor will share CIDRs, FW rules, SIEM endpoints. We'll do follow-up on KMS integration. 00:17:10 Samantha Lee: Sounds good. 00:17:12 Daniel Wu: Any other open items? 00:17:15 Maria Torres: Not from me. Thanks everyone. 00:17:18 Liam Chen: Thank you - we'll follow up in email with links and dates. 00:17:22 Zoe Martin: Thanks all. 00:17:25 [call ends - transcript truncated for brevity but full recording saved in the meeting artifact link] 00:17:30 NOTES: Shared artifacts: runbook link (https://redwood.s3/harbor/private-vpc-runbook.pdf), SOC2 summary (attached), security addendum (draft). 00:17:42 END OF TRANSCRIPT (Transcription contains occasional recognition errors for product names; timestamps approximate - full audio recording preserved.)
